items.title: Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained and Our Biggest Burning Questions
items.excerpt: We've got some questions about Godzilla Minus Zero, as well as how it might set up a third installment in the series.
items.content_text: You want to know if Godzilla Minus Zero has any post-credits scenes, don't you? We'll tell you right here: It does not. Though there is a short audio surprise for those who stick around to the end. Spoilers follow! It’s time to go go Godzilla , because Godzilla Minus Zero is now in theaters. The sequel to 2023’s instant classic Godzilla Minus One, Minus Zero reunites director Takashi Yamazaki and his cast for a new adventure featuring the Big G. The film is entering its opening weekend with strong reviews , including a 7/10 from IGN’s Scott Collura, who wrote that it “doesn’t disappoint in the slightest on the kaiju front.” Still, now that we’ve seen the film, we have some questions about certain plot elements and a potential third installment in the series. Let’s get into all the spoilery details of Godzilla Minus Zero. Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained We have a lot to get through, so we’ll keep the recap part brief. As indicated by the marketing, Ryunosuke Kamiki and Minami Hamabe return as Kōichi and Noriko Shikishima (they got married between films), who rejoin the civilian effort to protect postwar Japan from giant monsters, aka kaiju, while raising their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani). It’s now 1949 and the kaiju in question is King Ghidorah, an alien dragon who crashes on Earth inside a meteorite, and the plan is to use Noriko, who’s been infused with Godzilla cells from her encounter with the big guy in the last film, as bait to lure Godzilla into a fight with Ghidorah. While the ensuing battle (seemingly?) kills Ghidorah, it results in the death of Dr. Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), one of Kōichi’s allies from the first film, and also renders the Shikishima family fugitives from the occupying US military, who want to use Noriko’s Godzilla-summoning abilities as a weapon. More Minus Zero Godzilla Minus Zero Review Minus Zero Director Talks a Potential Godzilla Threequel Minus Zero Director Had to Avoid the Urge to One-Up Godzilla Minus One Minus Zero's Big, Brutal Climax Had a Household Inspiration There’s more to the movie’s story, such as meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), who uses her weather predicting powers to help the good guys (more useful than you might think), and Min Tanaka as Professor Murakami, an elderly biologist who builds the device Noriko uses to attract Godzilla’s attention. We’ll talk more about them in a bit. Overall, Minus Zero is a satisfying blockbuster for its kaiju action and endearing characters, and looks incredible on an IMAX screen. However, it’s not as tidy as the previous film, with a few things that left us scratching our heads once the credits started rolling. Namely… Did King Ghidorah Really Die? Let it not be said that Godzilla Minus Zero is lacking in spectacle, because the final showdown between Godzilla and King Ghidorah is one for the ages. However, the resolution is a bit strange because we’re not sure what happened to Ghidorah. The battle ends with the two monsters firing their energy beams at each other, and Godzilla’s seems to overpower his foe’s. But we don’t actually see Ghidorah’s fate. The edit here is weird, with Ghidorah just kind of disappearing between cuts; we don’t see a body, nor does he seem to explode into bits. So what happened? We know Ghidorah has incredible regenerative abilities, with him even being infected with Godzilla cells in the final fight (he starts growing Godzilla style dorsal fins while using his beam). Could Ghidorah have survived to menace the world anew? Or did Godzilla’s archenemy actually perish? It’s not quite clear, so we’d like to know! Why Did Professor Murakami Give Up on His Revenge? Professor Murakami is a new character in Godzilla Minus Zero, and one of the first people to witness and survive Ghidorah’s wrath. A biologist by trade, Murakami has cell samples of both Godzilla and Ghidorah, and also developed a machine that broadcasts a creature’s “resonance frequency” to draw more members of the same species to its location. Hooking Noriko up to the machine is what lets the heroes lure Godzilla to Ghidorah for the final battle. But Murakami has another use of the device: to get revenge for the death of his family in the bombing of Hiroshima. Halfway through the film, Murakami fantasizes about summoning Godzilla to New York City, where he annihilates Manhattan with an atomic blast. It’s an incredible scene, and paints what could be a fascinating direction for the movie to go… except it doesn’t. Murakami decides against revenge during the finale, and while Dr. Noda does go to him the night before and pleads for Murakami to give up on his vengeful crusade – Noda insists that “ending the cycle” of violence would be the true way to avenge his family – was that really enough to convince him? It feels like there’s a beat or two missing, some additional motivation for Murakami to change his path and destroy the device after Ghidorah’s defeat. The movie ends with Murakami as a prisoner of the US military, and he says there are “more minds to change.” Perhaps Murakami’s story will continue and we’ll get more light on his mindset if there’s a sequel. Does Doctor Aoyuma Have Magic Powers? This might seem like an odd question, but walk with me here. Makoto Aoyuma is a meteorologist who joins Dr. Noda’s Disaster Response Bureau, and her weather prediction abilities are surprisingly helpful in developing plans to counteract Ghidorah. She’s the one who suggests using lightning rods dropped from a bomber plane to strike Ghidorah down, and also uses storm patterns to track his movements so the Shikishimas can lure Godzilla to the right spot. That said, this is the 1940s, where weather prediction was much harder to do than it is now due to the limits of the era’s technology. There was even another movie this year, Pressure, a WWII drama about the meteorologists who helped plan the Normandy invasion, which showed how challenging forecasting the weather was at that time (it’s also a pretty good movie if you’re curious). But Aoyuma has an uncanny knack for it. The only time where she claims she’s failed with weather prediction in the past wasn’t even her fault. She got the forecast right, but people above her didn’t listen. There are even multiple scenes where Aoyuma sticks her head out into the air and seems to “sense” incoming weather like she’s a Jedi using the Force. So is Aoyuma just incredibly gifted in this field, or does she have some supernatural talent? The movie doesn’t say, but since there are psychics and fairies in other Godzilla movies, it wouldn’t be unprecedented. Was Ghidorah’s Arrival on Earth a Coincidence? To go back to other precedents in the Godzilla series, although the Minus films are more “realistic” than other interpretations, King Ghidorah is once again an alien in Godzilla Minus Zero. The perennial Godzilla nemesis is usually (but not always) from outer space and often works on behalf of invaders intent on conquering the world. While Ghidorah rides in on a meteorite, there’s no evidence in Minus Zero that it was purposefully sent to Earth by anyone. An invasion by Xiliens may be too pulpy for the tone of Yamazaki’s films, but Ghidorah just showing up only a couple of years after Godzilla and also just so happening to crash-land specifically in Japan is a remarkable set of circumstances. Is there more to Ghidorah’s arrival that we don’t yet know? Maybe this will be explored in another film if Ghidorah did indeed survive. Why Was Noriko the Only Survivor of Godzilla Cell Infection? As revealed at the end of Godzilla Minus One, Noriko was infected with Godzilla cells, which gave her enough regenerative ability to survive her injuries in that film. The infection expresses itself in Minus Zero as a discoloration of one eye and a patch of spikes on her right shoulder, which Noriko covers with an eye patch and bandage respectively. We later learn that Noriko was one of a handful of people infected with Godzilla cells, which initially results in a healing factor but then develops into mass mutations which can kill the host. In fact, Noriko is apparently the only person left with Godzilla cells who’s been able to survive long-term. So what makes Noriko so special? Is it just an unknown quirk of biology, or is there a greater explanation that Professor Murakami didn’t have time to study? Since Noriko is the only person who can power the “summon Godzilla” machine, we’d like to know more about how the infection works. Will There Be a Sequel to Godzilla Minus Zero? This is the big one. After two Godzilla films, Yamazaki has established himself as one of the best directors to ever tackle the big guy, but will there be a third entry in the series? Yamazaki has said he’s “fifty-fifty” on coming back for another film, so it’s not a guarantee. That said, Minus Zero ends on a note that could be developed down the line: the Shikishimas on the run from the US military, who want Noriko back so they can use Godzilla as a weapon. The thematic throughline of Minus Zero – that it is possible to sacrifice too much for the sake of an abstract “greater good” – is paid off by Kōichi and Noriko changing their minds about leaving Akiko at an orphanage for her safety and instead taking her with them to keep the family together, so it’s still a satisfying ending to this story. But with them riding off into the sunset, we can’t help but wonder: how far will the occupiers go to get Noriko back? Is there another adventure in showing the Shikishimas as fugitives staying one step ahead of a colonizing force who want to turn a country’s greatest trauma against the rest of the world? A sequel to Minus Zero (Godzilla Plus One?) would also give an opportunity to dig deeper into the other threads we’ve discussed. What does Yamazaki’s version of post-war Japan look like in the 1950s? Are there other monsters from the Godzilla franchise that could be revamped in this style? Could a third movie be even louder in IMAX? Honestly, Godzilla is an endless well for potential reinvention, so we hope to see many more movies about him in the years to come. What were your biggest questions coming out of Godzilla Minus Zero? Let us know in the comments! Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .

items.title: Avery the Poké Kid's Father Pleads With The Pokémon Company to Make a Trading Card in Honor of His Late Son
items.excerpt: The father of late Pokémon influencer Avery the Poké Kid is asking The Pokémon Company to create a special card in honor of his son.
items.content_text: The father of late Pokémon influencer Avery the Poké Kid is asking The Pokémon Company to create a special card in honor of his son. Avery the Poké Kid was a prominent and cheerful voice in the Pokémon Trading Card Game community. He died in September 2026 at 12 years old in after a seven-year-battle with pancreatic cancer; he went viral posthumously when his family shared a video of his final card pack opening a few days after his death, in which he excitedly pulled a 30th Anniversary Jirachi SIR card. Now, his father is putting forth a public request to The Pokémon Company to make a special card in Avery’s honor. On November 6, Christian Garcia — Avery’s father — published a tearful video on Instagram with a special plea to "immortalize" his son in the hobby he loved the most. “Trying to figure out how to carry on Avery’s legacy has been the biggest challenge of the last couple months,” Garcia said. “…I want to make a plea to anyone, literally anyone from The Pokémon Company: If you’re watching this video, I want to figure out how to immortalize him somehow in the trading card game he loved so much. “That kid literally was the embodiment of a Pokémon Master, and we’re hopeful, and I think it would be the coolest thing to open up a pack of cards and chase our son. If someone at The Pokémon Company is watching, please get a hold of us.” Fans and fellow collectors are doing everything they can to get the attention of The Pokémon Company, with most agreeing that it would only make sense to make his card some iteration of a Jirachi, given his viral pull that took over social media after his death. Avery’s heartbreaking Jirachi pull even caught the attention of the card’s artist, who posted an emotional reaction to the news on her Twitter/X account. “I’m so deeply moved. I’m so glad I kept drawing. I’ve honestly been in tears ever since I saw this,” she wrote. “‘I want my art to bring happiness to people.’ That’s one of the reasons I draw. I’m so glad I put that wish into this piece.” This latest statement from Avery’s father follows a September announcement from the influencer’s family in response to scalpers inflating the price of the 30th Anniversary Jirachi SIR card as a result of his viral video. “We are not involved in or benefiting from any cards being sold in Avery’s name or likeness. We have not approved these sales. We have asked sellers to take their listings down. Please do so immediately. This does not honor Avery’s generous heart. We are mourning our son and caring for our children. Please let us do that in peace,” they wrote at the time.

items.title: Pokémon TCG: 10 Most Valuable Delta Reign Cards From New Expansion
items.excerpt: Mega Rayquaza ex leads the secondary market surge in the newest Pokémon TCG expansion. Here are the 10 most expensive Delta Reign cards on TCGplayer and eBay.
items.content_text: The Pokémon Company International has officially unleashed Delta Reign - the all-new Pokémon Trading Card Game expansion that finally brings Mega Rayquaza back to tabletop prominence after a long five-year absence since its iconic run in Evolving Skies. That Rayquaza VMAX (Alternate Art Secret) from Evolving Skies chase card is still one of the most iconic cards of all time , currently sitting at a high of $1,044.19 on TCGplayer . As collectors race to collect all 141 cards and chase the set's heaviest hitters, the secondary market is already experiencing severe turbulence. To help you navigate the chaos of Delta Reign’s soaring valuations , we’ve broken down the 10 most expensive cards you can pull in the Delta Reign expansion, according to third-party market TCGPlayer. Kecleon - 117/103 This vaguely suggestive card of a Kecleon sliding down a pole, illustrated by Tomokazu Komiya, has proven to be a bit divisive; not everyone is a fan. I, personally, love the Art Brut-esque art style - it reminds me of colored pencils and crayons, when I would draw all my beloved Hoenn team as a child playing through Pokémon Emerald. This card can be yours for $16.93, falling from an initial launch price of $25.17. This is a great budget option, and one of my favourites in Delta Reign. Growlithe - 106/103 Illustrated by Yoshimoto Yoshimon, who you might know for heavy-hitters like Marill and Slurpuff from Ascended Heroes, this sweet Growlithe card got the ultimate cozy treatment in this adorable new Illustration Rare. Sat chilling in a pink, sunlit living room, you can almost imagine Growlithe basking in the sun, soaking in those final rays of the day. With a semi-translucent outline around this original 151 fire pup, it almost looks like a sticker. You can pick this up on release day for $17.67 from TCGPlayer - the price is already falling from a high of $18.92. Mega Golisopod ex - 135/103 This dynamic, colorful card from 5ban Graphics is coming in at number 8 on the most expensive cards of Delta Reign so far. The market average price is sat at $22.12, falling from an initial $23.24. Groudon - 111/103 This awesome Illustration Rare from Ryota Murayama shows off the continent Pokémon in all its glory. It packs a competitive punch too, dealing an extra 170 damage if a Stadium card with "Legendary" in its name is active. If its current market average of $28.43 is a little too steep for your liking, or if you just played Pokémon Sapphire as a kid, Kyogre is only $0.44 despite being a similarly gorgeous card. Eevee - 114/103 If there’s one thing you should know about me, it’s that I’m a big Eevee fan . So much so that I have over 200 Eeevee plushies in my bedroom. Yes, it’s becoming a bit of a problem. I adore this card from Hideki Ishikawa, showing Eevee in an adorable picnic scene for $30.37. If I lived in the world of Pokémon, I like to think this card is a snapshot of what my life would look like. Mega Golurk ex - 137/103 This card from 5ban Graphics has shot up in price since launch - it launched at $23.24, and now sits at $43.99. It’s no surprise really, when you consider the popularity of Mega Evolutions and their relative newness to the TCG. If you’re a big Mega Golurk fan, you should consider picking this card up sooner rather than later - I wouldn’t be surprised if it starts to spike again. Zinnia's Trust - 140/103 The Zinnia's Trust Special Illustration Rare, illustrated by GIDORA, just misses out on the top 3 spot. As the devoted Lorekeeper of the Draconid people, Zinnia’s connection to the Draconid legends and her efforts to summon Rayquaza to intercept the Grand Meteor Delta in Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire make her presence in an expansion anchored by Mega Rayquaza feel completely earned. You can pick this card up for $49.49. Raikou ex Taking the bronze Ribbon for the most expensive card in Delta Reign is this incredible Raikou Special Illustration Rare from aky CG Works. Raikou leaps through a jagged, towering canyon landscape that can’t help but remind me of Mt Thunder from Pokémon Mystery Dungeon Red/Blue games. Mega Rayquaza ex - 138/103 A hefty jump into second place here, and it’s no surprise which Mon takes home the silver Ribbons. This Mega Rayquaza ex Special Illustration Rare, illustrated by Kozuki Minami – the same artist that won the 2024 Pokémon TCG Illustration contest thanks to her inspired take on Pikachu, is currently sat at a market average of $334.82. Mega Rayquaza ex - 141/103 A fitting card to take home the Gold Ribbon, the Mega Ultra Rare Mega Rayquaza ex, illustrated by takuyoa, is, unsurpsingly perhaps, currently the most expensive card you can find in Delta Reign. TCGPlayer has one currently sold for $349.34, but the average price on eBay is sitting at an eye-watering $500. There are three total Rayquaza cards in this set if you’re looking to hunt them down - the 084/103 Double Rare, and the two mentioned in this list. There are some gorgeous cards in Delta Reign, and if you’re looking to hunt them down, your best bet is to hunt for Booster Boxes or ETBs at your local game store or online, as they offer the most consistent pull rates for the price. If you want a card in particular, I’d recommend waiting until the market settles so you can get the best value for money. Which card you you hoping to add to your binder? I'll definitely be keepng an eye out for the Eevee card as I mentioned. I also love the Kyogre card, and for that price, you can't really go wrong. There are some really nice cards in this set , and it's shaking out as one of the more affordable ones of recent memory. Happy hunting, Trainers!

items.title: Godzilla Minus Zero Director Takashi Yamazaki Explains the Household Inspiration for the Film’s Big, Brutal Climax
items.excerpt: Godzilla Minus Zero director Takashi Yamazaki says that he used his two cats fighting as the inspiration for the bloody brawl between Godzilla and King Ghidorah.
items.content_text: Warning! Spoilers ahead for Godzilla Minus Zero . Godzilla Minus Zero has the most viscerally violent kaiju battle since Gareth Edwards’ 2014 Godzilla . I’d say it easily surpasses that , even with Godzilla’s atomic-heat-ray-down-the-throat finishing move against the bug-like MUTO in Edwards’ movie that rebooted Toho’s franchise after 10 dormant years. In Godzilla Minus Zero, the inevitable showdown between Godzilla and the terrifying three-headed King Ghidorah is a bloody no-holds-barred melee from the get-go, with the two immediately going for each others’ jugular (or whatever the equivalent anatomy is of unknowable monsters from the sea and space). It’s not outlandish to call their fight the most intense monster-on-monster violence portrayed in the franchise’s history. Like Ken Watanabe’s character says in Edwards’ Godzilla, “Let them fight.” More Minus Zero Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained and Our Biggest Burning Questions Godzilla Minus Zero Review Minus Zero Director Talks a Potential Godzilla Threequel Minus Zero Director Had to Avoid the Urge to One-Up Godzilla Minus One How did writer/director Takashi Yamazaki think about staging this huge, all-out, flesh-ripping, head chopping, arm-tearing kaiju brawl? “So, I have two cats,” Yamazaki told IGN. “And for the most part, they're very nice and playful with each other, but on a rare occasion I think there's like — I don't know if they're crossing the line between play and actual fighting. I see two creatures fighting each other and I tend to think about my cats when that happens.” Incredible. Anyone with multiple cats knows exactly what Yamazaki is talking about, and the inspiration is hard to unsee. Ghidorah, even from his first scene of destruction, comes off as somewhat cat-like as he peeks at fleeing people in between buildings, like a cat hunting, before razing the city with his terrifying zaps of thunder breath. Then when he’s done, he goes and curls up to take a long nap in a kaiju-sized bed, also known as a mountain crater. Like so many of the devastating human elements of Godzilla Minus Zero, the battle scene between Godzilla and Ghidorah takes full advantage of its R rating, the first for a Godzilla film. (Another first: It’s the first time a Japanese film was shot for IMAX.) Making the climax as gory and exciting as it is started all the way back at the script phrase. “When writing the screenplay for Godzilla Minus Zero, I remember writing, ‘This is a fight to the death.’ There was a duel between two of them and a fight to the death means one will inevitably die,” Yamazaki said. “Thinking about these two beasts that are equipped with the ability to kill each other and if they really go at it, what will happen? Even in nature, you start ripping parts of flesh off and then start to weaken your opponent to the point where you can deliver the finishing blow. So it felt natural that kaiju would also behave similarly in a fight to the death. “Thinking about this idea that one will inevitably die, I think it's impossible not to think about the sort of chaos that would ensue. But at the same time, I think it's sort of painful and sad to watch because I look at Godzilla and it almost feels like a cat being bullied in a way. And I think since having two cats and watching them so often, I've had this sickness where anything fighting looks like two cats fighting to me.” Godzilla Minus Zero opens in U.S. theaters on November 6. We liked its "satisfying and visually amazing scenes of giant-monster destruction" in our review . For more Godzilla, read about how Yamazaki told us that focusing on trying to one-up the Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One in this sequel was a surefire way to “risk diluting what makes the movie great in the first place.” The writer/director is still on the fence about turning his Godzilla movies into a trilogy. Image credit: Toho
